extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, literary critics, humor theorists, comic artists interested in theoretical foundations of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Henri Bergson's theoretical criteria for what makes something comic (the laughable), with examples and guidance on how those elements operate in forms, movements, situations, words, and character. Useful for analyzing or producing comic effects grounded in Bergson's essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic confined to the human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN; you may laugh at an animal or an object only because you detect in it some human attitude, expression or the human caprice that fashioned it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laughing at a hat is actually laughing at the human shape or caprice it embodies. If the element has no human stamp, it will not be laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / indifference as precondition
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter usually accompanies an ABSENCE OF FEELING — the comic demands a momentary anesthesia of the heart; it appeals to intelligence, not to emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot laugh (fully) while pitying or feeling deeply; to perceive the comic one must temporarily 'put our affection out of court and impose silence upon our pity.' Anti-pattern: trying to make an audience laugh while they are emotionally moved in the opposite direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social nature / need for an echo
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is essentially social — it 'appears to stand in need of an echo' and is always the laughter of a group; comic effects often depend on shared customs and collective imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: jokes that succeed in a full theatre may fail for an isolated listener; many comic effects do not translate between cultures. Production note: consider audience membership and shared references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical inelasticity / automatism (central law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element consists in a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY — where living flexibility is expected, we perceive rigidity or automatism (continuing a movement when circumstances call for change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who falls, a victim of a practical joke, the absent-minded person, or characters whose behaviour is governed by fixed habits. Bergson frames this as the leitmotiv: rigidity, automatism, and inelasticity produce the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression from accidental to integral comic (embedded automatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mechanical/accidental cause becomes intrinsic to the person (absentmindedness or a fixed idea), the comic penetrates the character itself and produces a coherent, cumulative hilarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: someone who becomes absorbed in romances and acts as a somnambulist (Don Quixote) — the comic effect intensifies when we can reconstruct the cause and see the behavior grow logically from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law: the more natural the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comic effect has an origin that seems natural, familiar or intelligible, the effect is more laughable; knowledge of the cause and its life-history increases hilarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: absentmindedness as a basic human tendency is funnier when shown arising from a concrete passion or fixation. Production tip: build a believable cause for behavior to heighten comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice = external/ready-made rigidity (versus tragic vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices that make us laugh are those 'brought from without' — ready-made frames or rigid habits that simplify and stereotype the person, rather than being fully incorporated tragic passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequent aesthetics: comedies often bear common-noun titles (Le Jaloux, L'Avare) because the vice stands out as an independent mechanism. Comic function: such vices are subject to corrective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic physiognomy: fixed grimace and lack of mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable facial expression is one that promises nothing more than it gives — a unique and permanent grimace suggesting rigidity, as if the person's whole moral life had crystallised into a particular cast of features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction from ugliness: comic relates more to rigidity than to mere ugliness. Examples: faces that seem always to be crying, laughing, whistling — these are comic because they suggest a stereotyped mechanical action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature principle: magnify latent tendency in the direction of movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature succeeds when exaggeration makes visible an already-existing embryonic distortion or tendency in the subject — the artist 'makes his models grimace, as they would do themselves if they went to the end of their tether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: exaggeration for its own sake is not comic unless it uncovers a natural inclination; good caricature respects the 'ground plan' of the feature and amplifies its implied movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures and movements are laughable in proportion to their machine-likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE — especially when a gesture is stereotyped, repetitive, or evidently automatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a public speaker with recurrent identical head or arm movements; imitation of gestures makes them laughable because imitation exposes their mechanical uniformity. Production tip: repeat a movement predictably to evoke automatism (but use with care).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / stereotypy as comic trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the same movement or phrase, contrary to the living variety of inner states, reveals automatism and invites laughter when the audience 'waits for it and it occurs when I expect it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: recurring catch-phrases, fixed gestures. Anti-pattern: overuse can dull the effect; the comic arises from perceiving life reduced to mechanical repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as disclosure of automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: To imitate someone is to make manifest the mechanical element that has crept into their person; imitation is intrinsically laughable because it isolates what is imitable (i.e., the non-living, repetitive part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mimicry shows how gestures have become separable from the living personality; production: mimicry/parody should focus on the mechanical core of behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical-occupation association as a comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Deflecting a gesture—without altering its form—towards some simple mechanical occupation (sawing wood, striking an anvil, tugging a bell-rope) makes it appear more frankly mechanical and increases comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a favored device of parody and clowning. Use concrete mechanical analogues to reframe human gestures as operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension and elasticity (social standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Life and society require TENSION and ELASTICITY (alert attention and adaptability); comic rigidity signals lack of these qualities and thereby marks an inadaptability to social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society's corrective: laughter functions as a social gesture that warns against eccentricity and encourages reciprocal adaptation. Use in analysis: consider how a comic element signals failed social responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social corrective / utilitarian aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a SOCIALLY SIGNIFICANT gesture: by the fear it inspires it restrains eccentricity and 'softens down' mechanical inelasticity; it pursues a utilitarian aim of general improvement while retaining an aesthetic dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive note: Bergson emphasizes the social utility of laughter (non-material repression) — treating laughter as sanction that promotes sociability and corrects manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic requires appeal to intelligence not emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce the full comic effect one must call 'into play nothing but their intelligence' — laughter's appeal is to detached comprehension rather than to moved feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: comedic constructions that aim primarily at intellectual recognition (seeing the mechanism, cause, or rigidity) will align with Bergson's model; those appealing chiefly to sentiment may not elicit true laughter.
